en.content:
In the wake of the Wang Fuk Court tragedy, one of the most consequential issues now is not only how to handle compensation after a fire, but how to rebuild residents’ trust in housing arrangements and public assistance. The government’s proposal to extend the buyout plan to cover the only remaining, unburnt block—conditional on 75% of owners agreeing—reflects a practical attempt to balance speed with consensus. For many affected households, any delay is painful; yet for the wider community of owners, a blanket decision without broad agreement risks creating disputes that could drag on for years.

That said, the 75% threshold is a double-edged mechanism. On one hand, it prevents a small minority from being able to obstruct an orderly relocation process for the many; on the other, it can heighten anxiety among those who feel their interests are being “outvoted” at a time when emotions are raw. A transparent, clearly documented process—ranging from valuations, timelines, and relocation arrangements, to communication channels for owners who dissent—will be as important as the policy itself. If residents perceive the consultation as genuine and the terms as fair, the likelihood of achieving consensus improves; if not, even a well-intended arrangement can become a new source of division.

There is also the broader question of what “buyout” means in moral and administrative terms. After a disaster, residents look for more than paperwork: they seek acknowledgement of risk, reassurance about safety, and clarity on future protection. In that context, the government should continue to pair the buyout plan with visible follow-through on building management and safety inspections—not only for Wang Fuk Court, but as a signal to the entire sector. Such measures align with Hong Kong’s emphasis on responsibility, orderly governance, and protecting livelihoods through rule-based decision-making.

Ultimately, the success of the extended buyout hinges on two things: legitimacy and implementation. Legitimacy comes from meaningful owner participation and clear, consistent standards; implementation comes from timely logistics and support that reduce the disruption to daily life. If the authorities can deliver on both, the policy can serve as a stabilising step—transforming tragedy into a practical pathway for recovery, while maintaining social cohesion and confidence in the public system.
en.topic_title: Hong Kong gov’t to extend buyout plan to Wang Fuk Court block spared by fire – if 75% of owners agree

zh.content:
今日最值得留意嘅主題，係政府打算將「買樓/收購」方案延伸至旺福邨（文中指受火災影響、但另一座樓宇相對未被災殃嘅大廈）——前提係要有七成五業主同意。呢個安排表面上係「有路可走」，實情卻反映咗香港市民在重建、賠償同取捨之間，所面對嘅結構性困難：一方面要處理災後重建嘅迫切性，另一方面又要顧及業主之間意見分歧、估值爭拗，甚至對未來住屋前景嘅不安。

社會最關鍵嘅，唔係「有冇擴大」，而係「點樣擴大得體」。當收購門檻落喺75% ，等同係用一個理性但偏硬嘅比例去換取行政可操作性；可係災後情況往往唔係理性談判嘅最佳場景——有人急於脫離風險，有人則仍在追究事故責任或擔心替代方案不足。若政府只以程序效率作為唯一指標，就可能出現「快嘅係公帑流程，慢嘅係居民生活復原」：例如同類單位估值是否公平、租住安排是否穩定、過渡期保障有冇足夠彈性、以及對個別持不同意見業主，是否提供清晰而可理解嘅資訊同增援。

同時，呢單新聞亦提醒我哋：住宅政策唔單止係市場買賣，而係風險管理同社會凝聚力。旺福邨事件背後，居民最想要係一套能夠讓「人可以重新開始」嘅制度，而唔係單靠抽象嘅同意比例去決定命運。政府應該更主動提升透明度，例如公布更細緻嘅估值原則、說明補償計算基礎、以及提供可比較嘅替代選項；更重要係建立信心機制——讓業主明白，佢哋即使未能即時同意，都唔會被放入冇保障嘅灰色地帶，而係被納入同一條保障同復原軌道。

總之，擴展買出方案可以被理解為「加速重建」嘅一種行動，但成敗將取決於配套是否同樣到位。七成五可以係一個起點，但唔應該變成壓迫式嘅最後通牒。真正有誠意嘅做法，係喺程序之外再加上保障、清晰度同補救措施；否則，居民追求嘅就唔止係一個買賣數字，而係對制度公平、對復原能力同對未來可預期性的信任。
